Title: Cato CTRL Research on Suspected Iranian MuddyWater Activity Using Israel Tax Authority Lures and SimpleHelp
Context: The table below maps vendor-documented features to potential attacker use and business impact
Full Text:
Executive Summary

We investigated a campaign targeting Israeli organizations through phishing emails impersonating the Israel Tax Authority. The activity has been observed since September 2026. Government-themed domains and a verification page lead recipients to ZIP archives containing executables disguised as tax-related documents. The campaign abuses SimpleHelp, a legitimate remote monitoring and management tool, to enable attacker-directed remote access.

The lure exploits a routine business task and can reach finance, accounting, and administrative staff across sectors. We suspect a connection to MuddyWater based on its documented use of SimpleHelp and targeting of Israel.

Key Findings

The campaign uses Israel Tax Authority impersonation and government-themed domains to distribute ZIP archives to Israeli organizations.

The payload is presented as a tax-related document but is a SimpleHelp executable.

Cato telemetry recorded threat prevention alert against campaign web infrastructure. The event demonstrates prevention of that request, without establishing a completed remote-access session.

Attack Flow

Figure 1 summarizes the delivery chain. Remote access depends on successful execution and activation of the SimpleHelp component.

Figure 1. Tax authority impersonation leads to a SimpleHelp executable. The dashed final step represents potential remote access following successful execution.

Technical Details and Analysis

This activity was previously described in public reporting by CyberIL. Our investigation examined the campaign’s delivery infrastructure and use of SimpleHelp.

From a tax themed email to a verification page

The attack begins with a phishing email impersonating the Israel Tax Authority. Recipients attempting to access the supposed personal area are directed to a lookalike site and prompted to complete a CAPTCHA-style verification step before downloading a ZIP archive.

The infrastructure uses names such as document-govil[.]com to resemble the official Israeli government namespace, gov.il. The string govil is part of a separately registered domain and does not indicate government affiliation.

The verification page in Figure 2 displays a checkbox, a Continue button, and the password 123123. This presentation reinforces the appearance of a protected document-delivery process.

Figure 2. Verification interface used in the tax authority lure.

A ZIP archive delivers the executable

Following the verification step, the download is presented as a tax-related archive. Figure 3 shows Israel_Tax_Authority.zip in the browser download history. The investigation also identifies an archive named document.zip.

Figure 3. Download of Israel_Tax_Authority.zip.

The agency-themed naming continues inside the archive. The executable shown in Figure 4 is named רשות המסים בישראל.exe, meaning “Israel Tax Authority.” A recipient expecting a tax document is instead presented with a program to run. The payload inventory also includes document.exe.

Figure 4. Executable named רשות המסים בישראל.exe presented under the tax authority pretext.

SimpleHelp provides the remote access capability

SimpleHelp is legitimate remote support software. In this campaign, it is used as the remote-access component behind the document lure. The research identifies 129.121.120[.]121 as associated command-and-control infrastructure.

Successful deployment can allow an operator to connect to the endpoint and continue the intrusion using the software’s built-in capabilities. The activity involved social engineering and abuse of legitimate RMM functionality. Our findings and SimpleHelp’s assessment are summarized in the disclosure section below.

Mapping the infrastructure with FOFA

We searched FOFA for the two observed HTTP ETag values. The search returned eight service records associated with 129.121.120[.]121, including records for document-govil[.]com and document-govil[.]online, as shown in Figure 5. Both domains displayed “Coming Soon” pages served by nginx.

Figure 5. FOFA results linking the two domains to 129.121.120[.]121. The eight results are service records on one IP.

Public reporting on SimpleHelp abuse

Group-IB previously documented MuddyWater’s use of SimpleHelp, providing context for our attribution assessment. Sophos, CISA, and Huntress have also reported separate ransomware incidents involving SimpleHelp exploitation or abuse.

Attribution Assessment

We suspect MuddyWater involvement based on the combination of Israeli organizational targeting, locally tailored authority impersonation, and delivery of legitimate remote-access software through phishing. HarfangLab documented an October 2023 MuddyWater phishing email linking to a SimpleHelp installer. Proofpoint documented Hebrew payroll lures in March 2024 that led Israeli recipients through PDF links to ZIP archives containing Atera installers.

Earlier campaigns also used institution-themed Egnyte subdomains and Hebrew filenames related to scholarships and tourism. These examples show a recurring approach of adapting recognizable Israeli identities and routine business tasks to persuade recipients to install remote-access software. The current campaign follows a similar pattern through Israel Tax Authority impersonation and tax-themed filenames.

The February 2022 joint government advisory identifies MuddyWater as a subordinate element of Iran’s Ministry of Intelligence and Security.

Disclosure Timeline

SimpleHelp is legitimate remote monitoring and management (RMM) software. Based on the evidence reviewed and validation with SimpleHelp, we did not identify exploitation of a SimpleHelp vulnerability or compromise of SimpleHelp’s own infrastructure in connection with this campaign. The activity investigated involved social engineering intended to induce users to deploy SimpleHelp configured to connect to attacker-controlled infrastructure, consistent with the broader abuse of legitimate RMM tools by threat actors.

SimpleHelp confirmed that both samples identify themselves as SimpleHelp Remote Access Client version 5.4.5. Based on the information we provided, SimpleHelp assessed the activity as apparent malicious use of an older release and stated that it had not seen evidence indicating exploitation of a SimpleHelp vulnerability. SimpleHelp offered to investigate associated infrastructure and assess available action, requesting server addresses or hostnames, observation timestamps, and supporting evidence through a private file request. We subsequently shared the relevant server list with SimpleHelp.

Title: See the Real AI Experience with Cato DEM
Context: From “AI Is Slow” to Knowing Where to Investigate Detecting poor performance is only the first step
Full Text:
AI is becoming part of everyday work. Employees rely on services such as ChatGPT and Claude to research, create, and solve problems, while developers increasingly use AI-powered tools like Cursor and coding agents in their development workflows.

As employees increasingly rely on AI to work more productively, the AI experience is becoming a critical part of the digital experience IT teams are expected to support. Slow responses, failed interactions, or inconsistent performance can disrupt workflows and undermine the productivity gains AI is meant to deliver.

The challenge is that IT may have limited visibility into the AI interaction itself. Teams may not know there is a problem until employees start complaining.

Cato Digital Experience Monitoring (DEM) addresses this visibility gap with AI Experience Monitoring, providing IT teams with live visibility into AI latency and failures, along with the context they need to investigate performance problems.

AI Is Becoming Critical to Everyday Work. Can IT See When It Fails?

As AI becomes embedded in daily workflows, its performance increasingly affects employee productivity. An employee waiting on ChatGPT or Claude, or a developer relying on an AI coding tool, expects that interaction to work quickly and reliably.

That creates a new digital experience for IT teams to support.

But knowing that an AI application is reachable does not necessarily tell IT whether the actual AI interaction is performing well. Teams may only learn about slow responses or failed interactions when a user opens a ticket saying, “Claude is slow today.”

Then the investigation begins. Is the issue associated with a particular AI service or model provider? Is it concentrated at a specific location? Does it affect users accessing the service in a particular way?

The challenge for IT is no longer simply whether employees can reach an AI service. It is knowing whether the AI experience is working well, before employees must tell them it isn’t.

Traditional Application Monitoring Can Obscure the Real AI Experience

Monitoring an AI application is not the same as monitoring an employee’s interaction with the AI model.

GenAI applications such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Cursor generate many different types of network traffic. The agentic portion of that traffic, including conversational interactions with AI models and traffic from coding agents, can be mixed with software downloads and updates, authentication requests, licensing and configuration calls, telemetry, and other background activity.

Measuring all this traffic together can create a noisy representation of the actual AI experience. For example, a large application download may affect usage figures even though it has nothing to do with an employee’s conversation with an AI model. Performance measurements can similarly mix model-provider latency with unrelated application activity.

As a result, IT can see application traffic without getting clean answers to two fundamental questions: How quickly is the AI responding, and how often are AI interactions failing?

To understand the real AI experience, IT needs to separate this AI traffic from the surrounding application noise.

Isolate the AI Traffic That Matters with Cato DEM

Cato DEM addresses this challenge with AI Agent Experience Monitoring.

Instead of treating all traffic generated by a GenAI application as a single experience, Cato isolates the AI portion of that traffic, the interactions with AI model providers, including conversational traffic and traffic from coding agents such as Claude Code. By separating these AI interactions from downloads, updates, authentication, telemetry, and other background traffic, Cato gives IT a clearer view of the experience that matters to users.

The capability focuses on two fundamental indicators: latency, showing how quickly the AI service is responding, and errors, showing how often AI interactions are failing.

IT can examine performance by application and model-provider domain to identify where degraded experiences are occurring. At launch, coverage includes ChatGPT, Claude, Cursor, and the OpenAI and Anthropic APIs, with additional AI services to be added over time.

And because AI Agent Experience Monitoring is built directly into Cato DEM, AI performance becomes part of the same digital experience monitoring environment IT teams already use.

Instead of waiting for someone to report that “AI is slow,” IT gains live visibility into the AI traffic itself.

From “AI Is Slow” to Knowing Where to Investigate

Detecting poor performance is only the first step. IT also needs context to narrow the investigation.

Cato provides a dedicated AI Agent Experience Monitoring drill-down, where teams can analyze latency and errors by model provider, domain, and site. They can also see how employees are accessing the AI service.

Cato DEM also shows how users access AI services, whether through a browser, terminal, script, or coding tool. For example, IT can distinguish between someone accessing Claude through a browser and a developer using a coding tool such as Claude Code.

Consider that complaint: “Claude is really slow today.”

Without AI-specific experience visibility, IT starts with a broad application-level investigation where model interactions are mixed with other Claude traffic. With Cato DEM, teams can focus on latency and failures in the actual AI traffic and then use provider, site, and client context to narrow the investigation.

This turns a vague user complaint into a much more focused performance investigation.

Cato DEM measures the network experience of that traffic; it does not monitor what an AI agent does.

Catch Poor AI Experiences Before They Become User Complaints

AI is becoming another digital tool employees rely on to get work done. Cato DEM gives IT teams the visibility to support that experience proactively.

Teams can identify slow AI interactions without background application traffic obscuring the picture. They can spot failed interactions through error monitoring. And when something goes wrong, the provider, site, and access context give IT operations and network teams a more focused starting point for troubleshooting.

Most importantly, this visibility lives within DEM alongside the performance data that the performance data teams already monitor. IT can extend the same operational approach used to support other employees’ digital experiences to AI services, making them part of everyday work.

As AI becomes increasingly important to employee productivity, waiting for users to report poor performance is no longer enough. Cato AI Agent Experience Monitoring helps IT see the real AI experience, so teams can find slow or failing AI before users must tell them something is wrong.

Title: Cato CTRL Threat Brief: eMudhra Certificate Compromise Highlights the Value of Protection Delivered by an AI-Native SASE Platform
Context: The post Cato CTRL Threat Brief: eMudhra Certificate Compromise Highlights the Value of Protection Delivered by an AI-Native SASE Platform appeared first on Cato Networks
Full Text:
Executive summary

Eight eMudhra intermediate certificate authority (CA) private keys were compromised after being generated with insufficient randomness. Attackers could use these keys to forge certificates and impersonate legitimate websites or services to clients that still trust them. An attacker able to intercept a connection could potentially read or modify sensitive traffic.

We have deployed a certificate-trust update through our centrally managed PoP architecture, removing affected eMudhra certificates from the trust store used for TLS inspection. Delivering the update through the Cato Cloud removed the need for customers to patch security appliances at individual locations.

What happened?

Intermediate CAs sign certificates used to authenticate websites and services. Compromising their private keys can enable attackers to issue fraudulent certificates for domains they do not control. Organizations can therefore face exposure even when their legitimate certificates come from another provider.

Google and Mozilla received reports on October 17, 2026, and distributed emergency certificate blocks that day.

Mozilla also released updates associated with CVE-2026-113470. These include the certificate block list directly in Firefox and Thunderbird, protecting installations even when automatic block-list updates are disabled or unavailable.

Google found that no website certificates issued through the six affected TLS intermediates had appeared in Certificate Transparency (CT) logs before its emergency block took effect. CT logs are public records of certificates. Browsers that enforce CT, including Chrome, require valid proof that a certificate has been submitted to these logs before accepting it. Those browsers would therefore have rejected fraudulent certificates from the affected intermediates even before receiving the emergency blocks.

However, this protection does not extend to all software. Some applications, older browsers, or configurations without CT enforcement may have accepted unlogged fraudulent certificates if they still trusted the affected intermediates. The absence of certificates from those intermediates in CT logs before Google’s block therefore does not prove that no attacks occurred.

eMudhra says its root private keys and other intermediate CAs are unaffected. Its investigation remains ongoing.

Business risks

The exposure extends beyond employee browsers. Applications, API integrations, containers, and embedded devices may use independent trust stores or lack effective certificate-revocation checks.

Potential business consequences include:

Credential theft and data exposure: Intercepted connections could expose passwords, session tokens, and confidential information.

Transaction manipulation: Attackers impersonating trusted services could alter business communications or API responses.

Service disruption: Emergency trust removal can also reject legitimate certificates. Google announced a broader root-removal rollout expected on October 27, requiring affected website operators to replace their certificates.

Operational costs: Identifying and updating separate trust stores across applications and infrastructure creates work and opportunities for missed remediation.

These are potential impacts, not evidence of observed exploitation.

Our response: centralized control, global enforcement

The Cato AI-native SASE Platform converges networking and security in a cloud-native service delivered through globally distributed points of presence (PoPs). Our Single Pass Cloud Engine provides integrated security enforcement, while centralized management allows us to deliver updates across our cloud infrastructure. This reduces the coordination and maintenance work customers would otherwise undertake across distributed security appliances.

Centralized operations also support controlled deployment. Our established PoP change-management practices include phased rollouts, validation, monitoring, and rollback capabilities to manage operational risk as the platform evolves.

What this means for our customers

We have centrally deployed a certificate-trust update across our globally distributed PoPs, removing affected eMudhra certificates from the trust store used for TLS inspection. Customers do not need to make configuration changes to receive this update.

Analysis of our data lake showed that the certificate chains affected by this update appeared in only a very small proportion of the network flows examined. Based on this limited usage, we expect minimal connectivity impact for customers.

For details about the update and potential connectivity impact, see the security update.

For locations or connections that access the internet outside our platform, organizations should apply the relevant vendor updates or extend our platform’s coverage so those connections are subject to our certificate-validation controls.

Title: Why so many AI security programs start with the OWASP Top 10
Context: What OWASP is The Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) is a nonprofit foundation with a global community of security practitioners
Full Text:
When an auditor or an RFP asks how your organization handles AI risk, the OWASP Top 10 lists are often a core part of the checklist behind the question. Cato AI Security is built to address the risks on two lists.

What OWASP is

The Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) is a nonprofit foundation with a global community of security practitioners. It publishes free security guidance, and volunteers lead its projects and local chapters worldwide.

Its GenAI Security Project publishes several lists. Two of the most widely used are the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (2026) and the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications (2026). Each list ranks the 10 most critical risks that an AI security program should cover. Many security teams treat the lists as an industry standard and plan their AI security work around them.

The LLM list covers applications with a model embedded inside them, where risks include prompt injection and sensitive data leaking in a response. The agentic list covers what changes once agents plan tasks and call tools on their own.

The OWASP lists give each AI Security team the same set of risks to work from:

App developers use them as a guide to the risks their applications should avoid.

Security vendors build their products around them.

Auditors use them to assess the risk in an AI platform.

Buyers use them to evaluate AI security platforms.

Mitigating those risks is a responsibility shared by the security vendor and the teams that build and run your AI apps and agents. A security platform can stop some risks on its own. Others also need work in the app, the data pipeline or the agent platform.

How Cato AI Security maps to OWASP

Cato AI Security covers the risks on both lists in three ways:

Direct protection: Cato stops the risk in line, before the AI application or agent acts.

Shared protection: Cato reduces the risk and works with your app developers on the rest.

Platform evidence: Cato logs every AI interaction in an audit-ready format, so your team can investigate and show auditors what happened.

Cato AI security runs AI Security for Users, Applications, and Agents with unified visibility, context, and control, so the same inspection and policy applies to every risk below. The OWASP risks fall into three groups.

Supply chain risks

AI apps and agents rely on models, MCP servers and skills that someone else built. If one of them is compromised, every agent that uses it inherits the problem. OWASP lists this as Supply Chain (LLM04) and Agentic Supply Chain Vulnerabilities (ASI04).

A security team can’t set a policy for tools it can’t see. Cato protects against supply chain risk by discovering MCP servers and skills connected to agents and coding tools, including ones IT never approved, and applying policy to each one.

Prompt injection and sensitive data exposure

Attackers can hide instructions in content a model or agent reads and make it act against your policy. Employees can also paste API keys or personal data into an AI app. OWASP lists these as Prompt Injection (LLM01), Agent Goal Hijack (ASI01) and Sensitive Information Disclosure (LLM02).

Cato AI Security protects against prompt injection and data exposure through runtime guardrails on AI agents and the custom applications your teams build. It inspects each prompt and response in line, along with the results tools send back to an agent. Cato blocks prompt injection and jailbreak attempts before the model or agent acts.

The same inspection finds sensitive data in prompts and responses and in files attached to AI apps.

Tool misuse and excessive agent access

An agent with access to tools can change records and run commands. If it has more access than it needs, one bad instruction can cause serious damage. OWASP lists these as Excessive Agency (LLM03), Tool Misuse and Exploitation (ASI02) and Unbounded Consumption (LLM06).

Cato AI Security lets your security team name the tools, MCP servers and skills an agent may use, and block or monitor each one. Your security team can also set limits on how much apps and agents spend on model usage.

Where your team’s work starts

Some risks sit partly outside the traffic path. For these types of risks, Cato AI Security works alongside your team or provides platform evidence:

Data and model poisoning (LLM05): Cato AI Security detects manipulated context in live interactions, while your data pipeline owners protect training and fine-tuning data.

Rogue agents (ASI10): Cato AI Security keeps an inventory of agent activity and applies policy to each agent in line, while your agent platform owns the kill switch.

Cato’s AI interaction logs sit beside network, cloud access security broker (CASB) and endpoint data on one platform, so an analyst doesn’t have to pull logs from separate tools to investigate.

Get the full mapping from your Cato representative

Talk to your Cato representative to receive the complete map of how Cato covers the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications and the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications. We’ll go through the OWASP lists with you and map them against the apps and agents you run today, one use case at a time. You’ll see our coverage for each risk and how we work with your team to mitigate each one.

Title: Cato AI Endpoint secures browser AI, desktop AI and coding agents on every endpoint
Context: Endpoint detection and response (EDR) hunts for malware, and a coding agent doing what it was asked isn’t malware
Full Text:
AI used to live in a browser tab. Today it also runs inside the apps employees use every day, like Copilot in Word, in dedicated apps like ChatGPT and in coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Cursor.

Coding agents work differently from chat apps. A chat app answers a question and waits. A coding agent is given tools and takes actions on its own, with the developer’s access.

So every endpoint is becoming an agentic endpoint. Your security team now needs to know what the AI on those endpoints does and whose data it touches.

Cato AI Endpoint is a lightweight client that secures AI in the browser, AI in desktop apps and the coding agents developers run locally.

Separate point products leave blind spots on the endpoint

Take two employees on an ordinary afternoon. Sam, a developer, asks a coding agent to tidy up a build.

The agent opens the project files and reads the passwords inside. Then the agent pulls in a tool or a skill your security team never approved.

Maya in finance pastes a customer list into the ChatGPT app because she wants a summary before her next meeting. Neither Sam nor Maya means any harm.

Most of today’s security tools miss both. Endpoint detection and response (EDR) hunts for malware, and a coding agent doing what it was asked isn’t malware.

The web filter watches the browser, and network tools see what leaves the endpoint.

Sam’s agent works inside the endpoint, so much of what it does doesn’t cross the network at all. Maya’s prompt does leave, but some AI desktop apps lock their connection to their own certificate (certificate pinning), so network tools can’t look inside their traffic. The customer list goes out, and your security team doesn’t see it.

Each of those tools still does the job it’s made for, but network security can’t see enough of the endpoint to control agentic AI.

Skills and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers are add-ons that give agents extra abilities, and skills and MCP servers that sit installed but unused still widen the attack surface. An employee installs a skill once and forgets it, but the agent decides when to use it. If that skill can make web requests, the agent can use it to send data anywhere without asking.

Adding another point product for each kind of AI doesn’t close the gap either. Each product leaves its own blind spots and splits policy enforcement across more tools.

Secure browser AI, desktop AI and coding agents together

Cato AI Endpoint protects local agents, desktop apps, embedded AI assistants and web AI traffic with a lightweight client, so teams deploy and manage fewer tools. Protection starts with knowing which AI is already on your endpoints.

Discover Shadow AI and Agents. Shadow AI is AI that employees use without approval. Cato AI Endpoint can find the AI applications, local agents, MCP servers and skills on your endpoints, so your security team knows what is in use and what to govern first.

Protect Prompts and Responses Inline. When Sam’s agent calls the unapproved tool, Cato AI Endpoint can block the tool before it runs. The rest of the agent’s work carries on.

Cato AI Endpoint doesn’t act while Maya types or pastes. When Maya sends the prompt, Cato AI Endpoint can inspect and block the prompt on the endpoint before the customer list reaches the AI model. Maya sees a pop-up saying company policy blocked the prompt, and her session carries on.

The same user interaction rule applies to AI in the browser and desktop apps, with no extra configuration. When a prompt is sent, the rule can monitor it, block it or anonymize it by swapping names and other sensitive data for placeholders. Coding agents get monitor and block controls, and your team manages browser, desktop and coding agent protection from one dashboard.

Add AI security without replacing your existing stack

You’ve invested in EDR, in SSE (the cloud security service that includes your web filter) and in a VPN, and you can’t afford to disrupt them. You also need AI protection now.

Cato runs alongside the existing security stack. Only AI application traffic goes to Cato, and all other traffic stays on your existing tools, so you can see the AI in use within weeks.

The Cato AI Endpoint client goes out through device management like any other app. Finding the agents on an endpoint requires no network change. If another SSE client already runs on the endpoint, your team sets up both clients to run side by side.

Catch risky agents and prevent unsafe actions

Blocking Sam’s tool stops one unsafe action. Your security team also needs to know which other agents, MCP servers and skills on your endpoints are risky.

The Cato AI Endpoint client gives each skill a risk finding with a block, monitor or allow recommendation. Verified remote MCP servers get a badge. Cato can also flag risky agents, MCP servers and skills before they act, so teams can fix the riskiest first.

A week later, when someone asks which AI touched customer data, your team opens one dashboard and finds Sam’s blocked tool next to Maya’s blocked prompt. Each shows the user, endpoint and data behind it. Endpoint and network AI events sit in the same platform and data lake, so they share context.

Sam gets a tidy build without the unapproved tool, and Maya’s customer list stays inside the company.

Full Text:
When a user says, “the application is slow,” IT has to answer a much harder question: where did the problem actually begin? The issue could be on the endpoint, local network, ISP, the network path, enterprise infrastructure, or application provider itself.

That investigation often takes time because teams have to reproduce intermittent problems, collect evidence from separate tools, and hand cases between endpoint, network, and application owners. By the time troubleshooting starts, the evidence behind a transient issue may already be gone.

Cato Digital Experience Monitoring (DEM) Root Cause Analysis (RCA) changes that workflow. RCA brings together the broad range of experience signals available across Cato DEM, along with additional context from the Cato Management Application (CMA), to identify the likely fault domain and give IT a clearer place to investigate next.

The result is a more evidence-driven troubleshooting process: less time assembling the story after the fact, clearer ownership when issues cross teams, and a faster path from a vague user complaint to a focused investigation.

When “It’s Slow” Doesn’t Tell IT Where to Start

To an employee, very different problems can feel exactly the same. A weak Wi-Fi connection, last-mile congestion, a network path issue, or SaaS provider degradation may all result in the same complaint: “It’s slow.”

For IT, the challenge is not simply confirming that the experience was poor. It is determining where the experience likely broke down and which team should investigate first. A single complaint can span multiple technology domains, while many monitoring tools expose only fragments of that path.

This is especially difficult with intermittent issues. A user may report a frozen video call or a slow application after the condition has already cleared. If the team must recreate the problem before it can collect useful evidence, troubleshooting starts with a disadvantage.

Cato DEM RCA Turns Evidence Into a Starting Point

Cato DEM brings Root Cause Analysis directly into the digital-experience workflow. Instead of leaving administrators to reconstruct the troubleshooting picture manually, RCA correlates endpoint, network, application, and historical path evidence in a single investigation.

The goal is practical: turn available telemetry into a defensible starting point. RCA helps administrators identify the likely fault domain and determine where to act next. That may mean resolving the issue within the current team or routing it once, with supporting evidence, to the team best positioned to investigate.

For help desk, network, and digital workplace teams, that can reduce repeated testing and avoid unnecessary back-and-forth between owners. The investigation begins with context that has already been captured, rather than with a fresh search for clues.

RCA is therefore not another silo of telemetry. It is the layer that makes DEM evidence more actionable.

New Evidence Makes RCA More Actionable

RCA already draws on a broad set of DEM and CMA signals. Network Adapter Metrics and Client Traceroute add two more sources of evidence to the same RCA workflow.

Network Adapter Metrics adds endpoint and local-connectivity context, including adapter type, BSSID, channel, noise, and signal strength. This helps IT assess whether local conditions such as Wi-Fi are contributing to a poor experience.

Client Traceroute adds historical hop-by-hop path evidence from the client. It can reveal latency, loss, and path behavior that might otherwise disappear before the investigation begins, making it particularly useful for intermittent and remote-user issues.

The important point is that administrators do not have to treat these as standalone diagnostics and manually correlate the results. Both enrich the same RCA workflow with additional native context.

From “Zoom Is Freezing” to a Focused Investigation

Consider a remote employee who reports, “My Zoom calls keep freezing.” Without correlated evidence, IT may need to test the device, Wi-Fi, ISP, corporate network, and application provider one at a time.

With Cato DEM, RCA can bring together Network Adapter Metrics, Client Traceroute, in-tunnel traceroute, UCaaS or Real User Monitoring experience data, and network and Cato context in one investigation. Instead of starting with every possible domain, the team gets a likely fault domain and a focused place to begin.

RCA can also look beyond the individual user who triggered the investigation. Correlating experience data from other users can help determine whether the issue is isolated or shared and reveal the broader blast radius of the problem. For example, the evidence may point the investigation toward local Wi-Fi conditions. In another case, path evidence may show that the issue should be routed elsewhere. Either way, IT can start from evidence rather than guesswork.

Less Detective Work Across the Network You Already Have

By preserving and correlating evidence, RCA can accelerate triage, clarify ownership, reduce unnecessary handoffs, and help restore user productivity sooner. The operational shift is simple: teams spend less time finding and assembling evidence and more time acting on it.

That value does not require customers to replace their existing network. Digital-experience issues often cross technology and network boundaries, and Cato DEM is designed to provide visibility and RCA across Cato SASE and supported third-party network environments.

Organizations can begin with a focused troubleshooting use case and expand the shared evidence layer over time. Cato DEM helps IT move from “something is slow” to “here is where to investigate” – with the evidence already in hand.

Title: Beyond Deployment: Evaluating the Operational Impact of an SD-WAN Refresh
Context: Can IT keep critical applications performing consistently
Full Text:
Many SD-WAN refreshes start with an expiring contract or edge equipment reaching end of life. But replacing the edge should not be the measure of success.

For network and infrastructure leaders, the real test is what improves after the refresh. Will the refresh put IT on another appliance cycle, or move the WAN to a cloud service? Can IT keep critical applications performing consistently? Can the WAN respond when network conditions change? Can the team support new locations and changing requirements without creating more operational work?

The answers depend on how the new WAN is built and run.

Decide first whether the WAN runs on hardware or in the cloud

An appliance-based refresh replaces old boxes with new ones. IT still patches that hardware at every site, and the replacement cycle starts again when the new boxes reach end of life.

A cloud-delivered SD-WAN moves routing and policy into a cloud service. The device at each site connects the site to that service.

With Cato Secure SD-WAN, the Cato Socket at each site connects automatically to the nearest Cato Point of Presence (PoP). The Cato SASE Cloud Platform handles routing and policy enforcement, and Cato maintains the software that runs it. New capabilities can reach every site through the cloud service without a hardware upgrade.

Where the WAN runs shapes the rest of the refresh. The next three sections cover application priority, path control, and day-two work, and each one depends on where the WAN runs.

When you compare SD-WAN options, start by asking whether the refresh puts IT on another appliance cycle or moves the WAN to a cloud service.

Application priority should follow traffic past the branch

SD-WAN can prioritize important applications and steer traffic across available links. But in many architectures, that prioritization stops at the branch.

Once traffic leaves the branch, the application still has to cross the middle mile (the long-haul path between sites and clouds) to reach another site, a datacenter, or the cloud. If bandwidth gets tight along that path, the priority IT set at the branch should still count.

With Cato Secure SD-WAN, IT defines application-aware quality of service (QoS) centrally. Cato applies that priority at the Cato Socket and within the Cato SASE Cloud Platform, so the priority follows traffic into the middle mile. Business-critical traffic can stay at the front of the queue when capacity runs short.

Next, ask whether application priority ends at the branch or follows the application across the WAN.

The WAN should improve the path applications take

Priority can’t fix a bad route, though. A critical application can have the highest QoS priority and still perform poorly if its traffic runs into latency and packet loss on a long route to the destination. Path quality is the second middle-mile problem, after priority.

Cato sends traffic over the Cato Global Private Backbone, which gives Cato more control over the path between sites, clouds, and applications than a WAN that depends primarily on best-effort public Internet routing. Cato monitors network conditions and can route around degraded links across backbone paths between Cato PoPs. Critical applications can keep performing when a backbone path slows down.

For SaaS and public-cloud applications, Smart Egress adds another routing choice. IT can define application-level policy so selected traffic exits from a Cato PoP close to the application instance serving the organization. The traffic stays on the backbone for more of the trip, so employees can see faster response times from those applications.

Then ask whether the WAN can improve the route to the application, or whether the middle mile stays largely outside its control.

A refresh should reduce day-two operations work

Much of the work in an SD-WAN lifecycle happens after deployment.

New branches, policy changes, software updates, troubleshooting, and changing bandwidth requirements all create ongoing work. If that work still happens box by box and site by site, a refresh may replace the hardware without changing the operating model.

With Cato Secure SD-WAN, IT manages routing and application policy centrally through the Cato Management Application, while Cato Sockets support zero-touch deployment at new locations.

Because the WAN runs as a cloud service, IT can spend less time on the patch and replacement cycles that appliance-based designs require.

Finally, ask how much day-two work each option still leaves with your team.

Measure the refresh by what improves after deployment

Newer edge infrastructure is the minimum an SD-WAN refresh should deliver.

Performance and operations are only part of the refresh decision. You also need to decide whether the WAN should secure remote users and cloud access, or leave that job to a separate security stack.

The right choice gives IT a WAN that keeps improving long after the new edge goes in.

Title: Why AI Red Teaming Belongs at the Core of Your AI Security Program
Context: Gartner’s 2026–2027 ThreatScape names AI application compromise and prompt injection among four critical threats where attackers hold a significant advantage
Full Text:
Enterprises are putting AI applications and agents to work on sensitive data and business workflows, while attackers look for new ways to manipulate the models and exploit the tools connected to them. Security leaders need to know whether those systems will hold up against a real attack, and AI red teaming gives them that answer by testing AI the way an attacker would.

What AI red teaming is

AI red teaming is the process of proactively testing models, agents, applications, and other AI systems to find the weaknesses an attacker could exploit. It simulates techniques such as prompt injection, jailbreaks, data leakage, and model manipulation to see how a system responds under pressure.

Because AI systems and the attacks against them change all the time, red teaming works best as a continuous loop: test real-world behavior, find what fails, use that evidence to strengthen the protections that guard AI in production, and test again.

Why AI systems need continuous testing

Attack methods keep evolving. Threat actors constantly develop new ways to manipulate models and abuse connected tools and APIs. Because these techniques evolve as fast as AI itself, a system that passed last quarter’s tests may not hold up against this month’s attacks. Security teams need to test continuously for new attack techniques, not just the ones they already know.

Model choices change the risk profile. As token costs shape decisions, teams may switch models to lower-costs, or alternatively, switch to more capable, or different models to better fit their AI application. Each switch can change how a system responds to attacks and which safeguards it needs.

What red teaming achieves

Done well, AI red teaming delivers two outcomes: reduced business risk and proof that your AI controls work.

Red teaming shows which weaknesses matter

Red teaming exposes weaknesses before attackers find them and shows which of those weaknesses matter most.

Not every unexpected model response is a real risk, and testing for weaknesses no attacker could realistically exploit wastes effort. Good red teaming focuses on the attack paths that matter for your applications and data and ranks findings by realistic impact, so teams can choose models and design guardrails that align with real risk.

Red teaming produces the evidence compliance teams need

Governance, risk, and compliance teams increasingly need evidence that safeguards withstand realistic attacks, that AI systems don’t expose sensitive or regulated information, and that each application aligns with internal policy.

Gartner’s 2026–2027 ThreatScape names AI application compromise and prompt injection among four critical threats where attackers hold a significant advantage. To counter them, Gartner recommends testing AI applications early and using the results to improve runtime controls.

Frameworks including the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications, the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications (2026), the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, MITRE ATLAS, and the EU AI Act also call for adversarial testing and ongoing evaluation. Red teaming produces the record these frameworks expect: what was tested, what failed, how risks were prioritized, and how the organization responded.

Red teaming shows where your AI can be exploited

Treating red teaming as a prelaunch checkbox leaves a gap between what was tested and what runs in production, because models and connected tools keep changing after launch.

A mature AI security program should include three layers of defense: discovery, posture control, and runtime guardrails. Discovery answers “What AI do we have?” Red teaming sits within posture control and answers the next question: “Where can it be exploited?”

Those results help teams choose models that fit their risk profile and design guardrails around proven attack paths instead of generic assumptions.

What to look for in AI red teaming

A strong AI red teaming approach should include:

Continuous, proactive testing that keeps pace as models and attack techniques change or new models are adopted.

Actionable risk visibility that prioritizes tests by exploitability and impact, so teams focus on the risks that matter when choosing models and designing guardrails.

Audit-ready reporting that maps results to the risk and compliance frameworks governance teams already use.

Integrated remediation that connects findings to the policies and protections that address them, without stitching together disconnected tools.

Research quality matters too. Generic prompt libraries catch generic problems, while testing built on new attack research catches the techniques advanced attackers use.

Cato connects red teaming to runtime protection

At Cato, we believe red teaming delivers the most value when it combines deep attack research with the platform that protects AI in production. That research comes from Cato AI Labs, the team behind EchoLeak, the first reported zero-click AI vulnerability in Microsoft 365 Copilot, and CurXecute, a remote code execution flaw in the Cursor IDE. The team turns discoveries like these into realistic attack scenarios and adds new techniques as threats evolve, so testing reflects how attackers actually operate.

Cato AI Red Teaming puts that research to work. It continuously tests AI models with context-aware adversarial scenarios, prioritizes findings by realistic risk, maps them to leading frameworks, and turns them into policy and model recommendations inside the same AI Security solution that protects AI interactions at runtime.

With testing and protection on one platform, security teams can find AI risk and close the gaps before attackers exploit them.

Title: Stopping destructive commands in AI agents
Context: Together, they can take an application offline, erase critical configuration, lock out the employees needed to restore service, and turn a routine task into an expensive incident
Full Text:
An engineer gives a coding agent a routine task: clean up an old test deployment.

The request sounds harmless, and the environment is cluttered with unused cloud resources, stale branches, and temporary credentials that should have been removed weeks ago. The agent gets to work.

It lists resources, identifies old infrastructure, and finds a deployment command. Then it sees a naming pattern that appears to connect the test environment to production. Trying to be helpful, the agent removes what looks unused, resets a repository to a clean state, and revokes access it believes is no longer needed.

None of those steps necessarily looks alarming on its own.

Together, they can take an application offline, erase critical configuration, lock out the employees needed to restore service, and turn a routine task into an expensive incident.

Agents do more than answer questions

That is the challenge of agentic AI: agents are valuable because they can act. They can run commands, change files, and update security controls. But that same ability to act can create real business risk.

Sometimes, the agent makes the wrong move while trying to complete a legitimate task. It follows an unclear instruction, misunderstands its environment, or chooses an efficient path that exceeds what its user intended.

Other times, the intent is malicious. A threat actor who manipulates an agent through a prompt, a tool, or untrusted content can use the same permissions and capabilities to cause damage. What begins as a simple request can become a path to service disruption, data loss, weakened security controls, or costly cloud activity.

Ungoverned agentic behaviors can lead to lost revenue, interrupted operations, exposed data, recovery work across multiple teams, and damaged customer trust.

Access controls do not answer every question

The natural response is to restrict the agent’s access. An agent should only have the permissions it needs. But access controls alone do not answer the full question: should the agent take this action now?

Agents are designed to complete objectives. If one path is blocked, an agent may look for another permitted route to finish the task: using a different command or API, switching to another tool or service, accessing a different file or data source, or asking another agent or user to perform the step. A policy that says “do not use this resource” may still leave the agent able to create the same harmful outcome another way.

Consider an agent that cannot delete a production environment directly. It may still be able to remove the credentials that keep it running, overwrite its configuration, reset its deployment state, or disable the protections around it.

The risk comes from the behavior the agent is about to carry out with its access, and the impact that behavior could have.

Not every destructive action should be blocked

Recognizing a harmful action depends on context. A command such as rm -rf is not automatically destructive. Deleting a temporary build folder may be normal. Deleting a directory that contains customer data is very different.

The same is true for resetting a repository, deleting infrastructure, removing access, or changing a security policy. The command alone does not reveal whether the action is appropriate.

And some high-impact actions are intentionally part of the job.

An IT team may ask an agent to revoke a departing employee’s access. Data teams may ask it to delete records that have reached the end of their retention period, and Cloud teams may ask it to retire infrastructure after a migration.

In these cases, simply blocking the action is not the answer. The organization needs a way to make sure the right person understands and approves the impact before the agent proceeds.

Context turns commands into informed decisions

Cato’s destructive commands detector evaluates the action in context before it is executed.

The detector examines what the agent is trying to do, what it is targeting, where the action is happening, whether it is authorized, how difficult it would be to reverse, and how widely the impact could spread.

This helps Cato distinguish normal automation from actions that create material risk.

Removing temporary files from a test environment can proceed. Deleting customer data from production deserves a different response. Revoking access may be the intended task, but it can still require confirmation from the user who requested it.

That is the difference between treating every delete command as a threat and applying the right level of control to the action at hand.

Put teams in control of agent behavior

When the detector identifies a risky action, teams can define what happens next.

Using destructive commands detection in custom policies allows teams to create rules that reflect their own environments, policies, and risk tolerance. These rules can apply differently to users, teams, and the apps that they use. For one team, deleting temporary test resources may be acceptable, only requiring a user notification before execution, or simply monitoring and logging the behavior. For another, any command targeting production infrastructure, customer data, privileged credentials, or security controls should be blocked immediately.

The goal is to apply contextual control before an action creates an incident, so agents doing routine work are not slowed down at every turn.

Combined with other detectors and runtime protections, destructive commands detection gives teams a more complete way to govern agentic AI. It helps teams see risky behavior and enforce the right response.

Agentic AI can bring real speed and scale to the business when teams let agents act within clear limits on the actions that can cause real harm.
